title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "A" Circuit
plain: The engine computer has lost a usable signal from the mass air flow (MAF) sensor, which measures how much air is entering the engine. Without it, the computer has to guess how much fuel to add.

causes.name: Unplugged, loose or corroded MAF sensor connector
Damaged wiring between the sensor and the engine computer
Blown fuse or bad power or ground to the sensor

checks: Make sure the MAF connector is fully plugged in and the pins are clean
Look over the wiring near the air box for chafing or damage
Check the sensor's power, ground and signal with a meter before replacing it
fix: Usually a connector or wiring repair, or a new mass air flow sensor if the sensor itself has failed.
drive: You can often drive gently to a shop, but it may run poorly. If the engine stalls, hesitates badly when pulling out or merging, or blows black smoke, keep trips short and avoid highways; a stall makes steering and braking much harder. Get it checked in the next few days.
test_first: Check that the MAF connector is seated and clean, test power, ground and signal wiring, and look for air leaks after the sensor before replacing the MAF.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "A" Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The air flow sensor is working, but its readings don't match what the computer expects for the engine's speed and load. Most often the sensor is dirty or air is sneaking in around it.

causes.name: Dirty or contaminated MAF sensor element
Air leak between the MAF sensor and the throttle body
Clogged or poorly fitted air filter
Vacuum leak or stuck-open PCV valve

checks: Inspect the intake tube and clamps between the air box and throttle body for cracks or loose fittings
Check the air filter and clean the MAF sensor with MAF-safe cleaner
Compare live MAF readings at idle and at higher rpm against the expected values
fix: Often fixed by cleaning the MAF sensor and sealing intake air leaks; replace the sensor if readings stay wrong.
examples: Often follows the use of an over-oiled aftermarket air filter that coats the sensor
drive: Usually drivable for now, but hesitation can be risky when merging or crossing traffic. Get it checked within a week or two. If it stalls, stumbles badly, runs very rough, or the check engine light starts flashing, get it looked at right away.
test_first: Inspect the air filter and intake duct for leaks, compare MAF readings to expected values at idle and under load, and smoke test for vacuum leaks before replacing the MAF.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "A" Circuit Low
plain: The air flow sensor's signal is lower than it should ever be, as if almost no air were entering the engine. This usually points to a wiring or connector problem, or a failed sensor.

causes.name: Loose, unplugged or corroded MAF connector
Large air leak after the sensor

checks: Check that the MAF connector is seated and the pins are clean
Inspect the wiring harness near the air box
Measure the sensor's power, ground and signal voltage
fix: Repair the connector or wiring, or replace the mass air flow sensor.
drive: You can often drive gently to a shop, but it may run poorly. If the engine stalls, hesitates badly when pulling out or merging, or blows black smoke, keep trips short and avoid highways; a stall makes steering and braking much harder. Get it checked in the next few days.
test_first: Check that the MAF connector is seated and clean, test power, ground and signal wiring, and look for air leaks after the sensor before replacing the MAF.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "A" Circuit High
plain: The air flow sensor's signal is higher than it should ever be, as if a huge amount of air were rushing in. This is usually an electrical fault in the sensor or its wiring.

causes.name: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Wiring routed too close to ignition parts or the alternator

checks: Inspect the MAF wiring for rubbed-through or melted spots
Check the sensor ground connection
Compare the signal voltage with the engine off and at idle
fix: Repair the shorted wiring or replace the mass air flow sensor.
drive: You can often drive gently to a shop, but it may run poorly. If the engine stalls, hesitates badly when pulling out or merging, or blows black smoke, keep trips short and avoid highways; a stall makes steering and braking much harder. Get it checked in the next few days.
test_first: Check MAF power, ground and signal voltage with the engine running, and look for wiring routed near ignition parts or the alternator before replacing the sensor.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "A" Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
plain: The air flow sensor's signal keeps cutting out or jumping around. That usually means a loose connection or a sensor that is starting to fail.
symptoms: Problem may come and go with bumps or temperature
checks: Wiggle the MAF connector and wiring with the engine running and watch for a stumble
Inspect the connector pins for corrosion or spread terminals
fix: Repair the loose connection or wiring; replace the sensor if the signal still drops out.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit
plain: There's an electrical problem with the MAP sensor, which measures the pressure (vacuum) inside the intake manifold. The computer uses it to judge engine load and fuel needs.

causes.name: Damaged or unplugged MAP sensor connector
Open or shorted wiring to the sensor

checks: Check the MAP sensor connector and wiring
Measure the sensor's reference voltage, ground and signal
fix: Repair the wiring or connector, or replace the MAP sensor.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The MAP sensor's reading doesn't make sense for how the engine is running. Often a cracked vacuum hose, a leak, or a lazy sensor is to blame.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose to the MAP sensor
Engine mechanical problem causing low vacuum

checks: Inspect the MAP sensor hose, seal or grommet for cracks
Compare the MAP reading with key on, engine off to the local barometric pressure
Check engine vacuum with a gauge
fix: Fix the vacuum hose or leak; replace the MAP sensor if its readings are still off.
examples: A cracked vacuum hose or worn sensor seal is a frequent trigger on older trucks
drive: Usually drivable for now, but hesitation can be risky when merging or crossing traffic. Get it checked within a week or two. If it stalls, stumbles badly, runs very rough, or the check engine light starts flashing, get it looked at right away.
test_first: Inspect the MAP vacuum hose, compare the MAP reading to barometric pressure with the key on and engine off, and check engine vacuum with a gauge before replacing the sensor.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit Low
plain: The MAP sensor signal is lower than its normal range, which usually means a broken wire, a bad connection or a failed sensor.

causes.name: Unplugged or corroded MAP sensor connector
Open or grounded signal wire, or lost 5-volt reference

checks: Check the MAP connector and look for damaged wiring
Confirm the sensor has its 5-volt reference and a good ground
Look for other codes that share the same 5-volt reference circuit
fix: Repair the connector or wiring, or replace the MAP sensor.
drive: You can often drive gently to a shop, but it may run poorly. If the engine stalls, hesitates badly when pulling out or merging, or blows black smoke, keep trips short and avoid highways; a stall makes steering and braking much harder. Get it checked in the next few days.
test_first: Check the MAP connector, 5-volt reference, ground and signal wires before replacing the sensor; a lost reference can also affect other sensors on the same circuit.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit High
plain: The MAP sensor signal is higher than its normal range. This often comes from a vacuum hose that has come off, a wiring short, or a failed sensor.

causes.name: Disconnected or split vacuum hose to the MAP sensor
Signal wire shorted to voltage or open ground
Very low engine vacuum from a mechanical problem

checks: Check the vacuum supply to the MAP sensor
Inspect the sensor wiring and ground
Check engine vacuum with a gauge
fix: Reconnect or replace the vacuum hose, repair wiring, or replace the MAP sensor.
drive: You can often drive gently to a shop, but it may run poorly. If the engine stalls, hesitates badly when pulling out or merging, or blows black smoke, keep trips short and avoid highways; a stall makes steering and braking much harder. Get it checked in the next few days.
test_first: Check the MAP vacuum hose, sensor ground and signal wire, and measure actual engine vacuum with a gauge before replacing the sensor.

title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Circuit Intermittent
plain: The MAP sensor signal is dropping out or jumping around now and then, usually from a loose connection or a failing sensor.
checks: Wiggle-test the MAP connector and harness while watching the live reading
Inspect the vacuum hose for cracks that open up when warm
fix: Repair the loose connection or wiring; replace the MAP sensor if the signal still drops out.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "B" Circuit
plain: Some engines use two air flow sensors. This code means the computer has lost a usable signal from the second one, called sensor B.

causes.name: Unplugged or corroded sensor B connector

checks: Find which sensor is B for your engine and check its connector
Test the sensor's power, ground and signal
fix: Repair the connector or wiring, or replace air flow sensor B.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "B" Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The second air flow sensor (sensor B) is sending readings that don't fit how the engine is running, often because it is dirty or there's an air leak.

causes.name: Air leak in the intake ducting after the sensor

checks: Inspect the intake ducting for cracks and loose clamps
Clean the sensor with MAF-safe cleaner and recheck readings
fix: Clean the sensor and seal any air leaks; replace the sensor if readings stay wrong.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "B" Circuit Low
plain: The signal from the second air flow sensor (sensor B) is lower than it should ever be, usually from a wiring problem or a failed sensor.
checks: Check the sensor connector and wiring
Measure the sensor's power, ground and signal
fix: Repair the wiring or connector, or replace air flow sensor B.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "B" Circuit High
plain: The signal from the second air flow sensor (sensor B) is higher than it should ever be, usually from a short in the wiring or a failed sensor.
checks: Inspect the wiring for rubbed-through spots
Check the sensor ground and signal voltage
fix: Repair the shorted wiring or replace air flow sensor B.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor "B" Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
plain: The signal from the second air flow sensor (sensor B) keeps dropping out or jumping around, usually from a loose connection.
checks: Wiggle-test the connector and harness while watching the live reading
Inspect the connector pins for corrosion
fix: Repair the loose connection or wiring; replace the sensor if the signal still drops out.

title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation
plain: On engines with two air flow sensors, the two readings should agree. This code means they disagree by more than the computer allows.

causes.name: One air flow sensor dirty or failing
Air leak in one side of the intake
Wiring or connector problem on one sensor

checks: Compare live readings from both sensors
Inspect both intake paths for leaks or blockages
fix: Clean or replace the sensor that reads wrong, and fix any intake leak.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit (Bank 1)
plain: There's an electrical problem with the intake air temperature sensor, which tells the computer how cold or warm the incoming air is so it can adjust fuel.
symptoms: Usually little change in how the car drives
Possible hard starting in cold weather

causes.name: Failed intake air temperature sensor (often built into the MAF)

checks: Check the sensor connector, which may be on the air box or MAF sensor
Read the live intake air temperature; it should be close to outside air on a cold engine
Check the wiring for damage
fix: Repair the connector or wiring, or replace the intake air temperature sensor (or MAF sensor if it is built in).
drive: Usually you can keep driving and schedule a repair. The car may start harder in cold weather or use a bit more fuel. If it starts running rough, hesitating or stalling, or other codes show up, get it checked sooner.
test_first: Compare the intake air temperature reading to outside air on a cold engine, and check the connector and wiring for opens or shorts. The sensor may be built into the MAF.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
plain: The intake air temperature reading doesn't make sense, such as not changing as the engine warms or not matching other temperature sensors after the car sits.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives
Possible slight drop in fuel economy

causes.name: Sensor mounted wrong or out of the air stream

checks: After the car sits overnight, compare the intake air and coolant temperature readings; they should be close
Inspect the connector for corrosion
Make sure the sensor is seated in the intake properly
fix: Usually a new intake air temperature sensor, or a MAF sensor where the two are combined.
drive: Usually you can keep driving and schedule a repair. The car may start harder in cold weather or use a bit more fuel. If it starts running rough, hesitating or stalling, or other codes show up, get it checked sooner.
test_first: Compare the intake air temperature reading to outside air on a cold engine, confirm the sensor is mounted in the air stream, and check connector and wiring resistance.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low (Bank 1)
plain: The intake air temperature sensor is reporting an impossibly hot reading. That usually means its circuit is shorted or the sensor has failed.
symptoms: Slight hesitation or lower fuel economy
checks: Read the live intake air temperature; a reading far above outside air on a cold engine points to a short
Unplug the sensor and see if the reading drops to a very cold value
Inspect the wiring for pinched or rubbed spots
fix: Repair the shorted wiring or replace the intake air temperature sensor.
drive: Usually you can keep driving and schedule a repair. The car may start harder in cold weather or use a bit more fuel. If it starts running rough, hesitating or stalling, or other codes show up, get it checked sooner.
test_first: Compare the intake air temperature reading to outside air on a cold engine, and check the connector and wiring for opens or shorts. The sensor may be built into the MAF.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High (Bank 1)
plain: The intake air temperature sensor is reporting an impossibly cold reading. Most often the sensor is unplugged, a wire is broken, or the sensor has failed.
symptoms: Possible rough running or lower fuel economy

causes.name: Sensor or MAF connector left unplugged or loose

checks: Make sure the sensor is plugged in, especially after an air filter change
Read the live temperature; a reading near minus 40 points to an open circuit
Check the wiring and connector for damage or corrosion
fix: Plug in or repair the connector or wiring; replace the sensor if it reads wrong with good wiring.
examples: Often appears right after an air filter change when the sensor or MAF plug is left loose
drive: Usually you can keep driving and schedule a repair. The car may start harder in cold weather or use a bit more fuel. If it starts running rough, hesitating or stalling, or other codes show up, get it checked sooner.
test_first: Compare the intake air temperature reading to outside air on a cold engine, and check the connector and wiring for opens or shorts. The sensor may be built into the MAF.

title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)
plain: The intake air temperature reading is jumping around or cutting out, usually from a loose connection or a sensor that's failing.
checks: Wiggle-test the connector and wiring while watching the live reading
Inspect the connector pins for corrosion
fix: Repair the loose connection or wiring; replace the sensor if the reading still jumps.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
plain: There's an electrical problem with the coolant temperature sensor, which tells the computer how warm the engine is. It affects fuel mixture, idle and often the cooling fans.
symptoms: Hard starting or rough running when cold
Temperature gauge reading wrong or not moving
Cooling fans may run all the time
checks: Check the coolant level first
Inspect the sensor connector and wiring
Compare the live coolant temperature reading with the actual engine temperature
fix: Usually a new coolant temperature sensor or a connector repair.
drive: Watch for real overheating, since this code can make the gauge read wrong. If you see steam, smell coolant, the gauge reads high or the cooling fans aren't running, pull over and shut it off. Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. Otherwise get it to a shop soon.
test_first: Compare the coolant temperature reading to actual engine temperature with an infrared thermometer, check coolant level, and test the connector and wiring before replacing the sensor.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The coolant temperature reading doesn't make sense, such as warming too slowly, jumping suddenly, or not matching other temperature sensors after the car sits overnight.
symptoms: Heater may be slow to warm up

causes.name: Low coolant or air pocket at the sensor
Corroded connector or high wiring resistance

checks: Check the coolant level and bleed air from the system
Compare the coolant and intake air readings after the car sits overnight
Watch the coolant temperature as the engine warms to see if it climbs steadily
fix: Usually a new coolant temperature sensor; replace the thermostat if the engine is slow to warm.
drive: Usually drivable, but the temperature gauge may not be reliable. Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If you see steam, smell coolant, the heater blows cold, or the fans stop working, pull over and shut it off. Otherwise get it checked within a week or two.
test_first: Check coolant level and for air pockets, compare the sensor reading to actual temperature and other temperature sensors, and confirm the thermostat works before replacing the sensor.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
plain: The coolant temperature sensor is reporting an impossibly hot engine. That usually means a shorted wire or failed sensor, but make sure the engine isn't really overheating.
symptoms: Hard starting or rough running when cold
checks: Confirm the engine is not really overheating and coolant is full
Unplug the sensor and see if the reading drops to a very cold value
Inspect the wiring for pinched or melted spots
fix: Repair the shorted wiring or replace the coolant temperature sensor.
drive: This code can come from a real overheat, so take it seriously. If the gauge reads high, you see steam or smell coolant, pull over and shut it off. Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. If the temperature looks normal and it runs well, get it to a shop soon.
test_first: Confirm the engine isn't actually overheating, compare the sensor reading to actual temperature, and check the signal wire for a short to ground before replacing the sensor.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
plain: The coolant temperature sensor is reporting an impossibly cold engine, usually because it's unplugged, a wire is broken, or the sensor has failed. The fans may not come on when needed.
symptoms: Temperature gauge stays low or reads cold
Cooling fans may run all the time or not at all
checks: Check that the sensor connector is fully plugged in and not corroded
Read the live coolant temperature; a reading near minus 40 points to an open circuit
Inspect the wiring along the engine for breaks
fix: Repair the connector or wiring, or replace the coolant temperature sensor.
drive: Watch for real overheating, since this code can make the gauge read wrong. If you see steam, smell coolant, the gauge reads high or the cooling fans aren't running, pull over and shut it off. Check the coolant level when the engine is cold. Otherwise get it to a shop soon.
test_first: Compare the coolant temperature reading to actual engine temperature with an infrared thermometer, check coolant level, and test the connector and wiring before replacing the sensor.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
plain: The coolant temperature reading is jumping around or cutting out, usually from a loose connection, a failing sensor, or air in the cooling system.
symptoms: Cooling fans switching on and off oddly

causes.name: Low coolant or air pocket at the sensor

checks: Check the coolant level and bleed air from the system
Wiggle-test the connector while watching the live reading
fix: Top up and bleed the coolant, repair the connection, or replace the sensor.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation
plain: Engines with two coolant temperature sensors expect them to read about the same. This code means the two readings disagree by too much.

causes.name: One coolant temperature sensor reading wrong
Low coolant or air trapped near one sensor
Corroded connector or high wiring resistance

checks: Check the coolant level and bleed the system
Compare both sensor readings on a cold engine after the car sits
fix: Replace the sensor that reads out of line, or fix the coolant level or wiring problem.

title: Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation
plain: After the car sits long enough to cool down, the coolant and intake air temperatures should be nearly the same. This code means they don't agree.
checks: After an overnight cool-down, compare the coolant and intake air readings to the actual outside temperature
Ask whether a block heater was plugged in before the code set
fix: Replace whichever sensor reads out of line with the real temperature.

title: Charge Air Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation (Bank 1)
plain: On turbocharged or supercharged engines, the temperature of the boosted air and the incoming air should agree when the engine is cold. This code means they don't.
symptoms: Possible reduced power in some cases
checks: Compare both temperature readings after an overnight cool-down
Inspect both sensor connectors for oil or corrosion
fix: Replace the sensor that reads out of line, or repair the wiring.

title: Charge Air Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation (Bank 2)
plain: Same as P011C but for bank 2: on a boosted engine, the charge air and intake air temperatures disagree when they should match.
checks: Compare both temperature readings after an overnight cool-down
Inspect both sensor connectors for oil or corrosion
fix: Replace the sensor that reads out of line, or repair the wiring.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch "A" Circuit
plain: There's an electrical problem with throttle position sensor A, which tells the computer how far the throttle is open. Many cars go into a reduced-power mode to stay safe.

causes.name: Faulty throttle position sensor or throttle body

checks: Inspect the throttle body connector and wiring
Watch the live throttle position reading while slowly pressing the pedal; it should rise smoothly
Check for related throttle or pedal codes
fix: Repair the wiring or connector, or replace the throttle position sensor (on most newer cars, the whole throttle body).

cost.job: Replace throttle position sensor or throttle body

drive: Limit driving. Throttle sensor faults can cause sudden reduced power, surging, a high idle or stalling, which is dangerous in traffic or when merging. If the car won't accelerate properly, surges on its own or stalls, don't drive it in traffic; have it towed or move it only a short distance.
test_first: Check the throttle body and pedal sensor connectors, 5-volt reference and ground, and compare sensor readings as the throttle moves before replacing the throttle body or pedal.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch "A" Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The throttle position sensor's reading doesn't line up with what the engine is doing, such as not matching air flow or the second throttle sensor. It often points to a worn sensor.

causes.name: Worn throttle position sensor with a dead spot
Air flow or MAP sensor reading wrong

checks: Watch the live throttle reading while slowly pressing the pedal and look for dropouts
Inspect and clean the throttle body
Check the connector for corrosion
fix: Usually a new throttle position sensor, or the throttle body on cars where the sensor is built in.

cost.job: Replace throttle position sensor or throttle body

drive: Limit driving. Throttle sensor faults can cause sudden reduced power, surging, a high idle or stalling, which is dangerous in traffic or when merging. If the car won't accelerate properly, surges on its own or stalls, don't drive it in traffic; have it towed or move it only a short distance.
test_first: Clean and inspect the throttle body, watch the throttle sensor signal for dead spots while sweeping it, and check MAF and MAP readings before replacing the throttle body.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch "A" Circuit Low
plain: Throttle position sensor A is sending a signal that is lower than normal, usually from a wiring fault, a bad connection or a failed sensor. The car may limit power.
symptoms: Idle may be high or unsteady

causes.name: Failed throttle position sensor or throttle body
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Lost 5-volt reference from the engine computer

checks: Check the throttle body connector and wiring
Measure the 5-volt reference, ground and signal at the sensor
Look for other codes sharing the same 5-volt reference
fix: Repair the wiring or connector, or replace the throttle position sensor or throttle body.

cost.job: Replace throttle position sensor or throttle body

drive: Limit driving. Throttle sensor faults can cause sudden reduced power, surging, a high idle or stalling, which is dangerous in traffic or when merging. If the car won't accelerate properly, surges on its own or stalls, don't drive it in traffic; have it towed or move it only a short distance.
test_first: Check the throttle body and pedal sensor connectors, 5-volt reference and ground, and compare sensor readings as the throttle moves before replacing the throttle body or pedal.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch "A" Circuit High
plain: Throttle position sensor A is sending a signal that is higher than normal, usually from a short in the wiring, a bad ground or a failed sensor. The car may limit power.

causes.name: Failed throttle position sensor or throttle body

checks: Inspect the throttle body connector and wiring
Check the sensor ground and signal voltage at closed throttle
Watch the live reading while slowly pressing the pedal
fix: Repair the wiring or ground, or replace the throttle position sensor or throttle body.

cost.job: Replace throttle position sensor or throttle body

drive: Limit driving. Throttle sensor faults can cause sudden reduced power, surging, a high idle or stalling, which is dangerous in traffic or when merging. If the car won't accelerate properly, surges on its own or stalls, don't drive it in traffic; have it towed or move it only a short distance.
test_first: Check the throttle body and pedal sensor connectors, 5-volt reference and ground, and compare sensor readings as the throttle moves before replacing the throttle body or pedal.

title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch "A" Circuit Intermittent
plain: Throttle position sensor A's signal keeps dropping out or jumping, usually from a worn sensor or a loose connection.
checks: Watch the live throttle reading while slowly pressing the pedal and look for spikes or drops
Wiggle-test the connector and wiring
fix: Repair the connection, or replace the throttle position sensor or throttle body.

title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control
plain: The engine is taking too long to warm up enough for the computer to start fine-tuning the fuel mixture. A thermostat stuck open is the usual cause.
symptoms: Temperature gauge slow to rise or stays low
Heater slow to blow warm air

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early
Cooling fan running all the time

checks: Check the coolant level
Watch the coolant temperature as the engine warms; it should reach normal within about 10 to 15 minutes
Check whether the cooling fan is running on a cold engine
fix: Usually a new thermostat; replace the coolant temperature sensor if it reads wrong.
drive: Usually drivable. The engine is running cooler than it should, so expect weak heat and slightly worse fuel economy. In cold weather a weak defroster can block your view, so get it fixed before winter. If the gauge ever reads high or you see steam, pull over and shut it off.
test_first: Check coolant level, compare the coolant sensor reading to actual engine temperature, watch how long warm-up takes, and confirm the fan isn't stuck on before replacing the thermostat.

title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Stable Operation
plain: The engine isn't staying warm enough for steady, efficient running. Most often the thermostat is stuck open or the coolant temperature sensor is reading low.
checks: Check the coolant level
Watch the coolant temperature during a drive to see if it stays below normal
fix: Usually a new thermostat; replace the coolant temperature sensor if it reads wrong.

title: Intake Air Temperature Too High
plain: The air going into the engine is hotter than expected. This often shows up on turbocharged or supercharged engines when the intercooler isn't cooling the air well.

causes.name: Intercooler not cooling (failed pump, low coolant or blocked fins)
Hot air being drawn in from a damaged intake duct

checks: Compare the intake air reading to outside temperature on a cold engine
On boosted engines, check the intercooler, its coolant level and pump
fix: Repair the intercooler system or air duct, or replace the intake air temperature sensor.

title: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
plain: The engine is taking too long to reach its normal operating temperature. In most cases the thermostat is stuck partly open and letting coolant cool the engine too soon.
symptoms: Temperature gauge reads lower than usual

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early
Wiring or connector fault at the temperature sensor

checks: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold
Watch the live coolant temperature on a drive to see if it reaches normal
Check whether the cooling fan runs when the engine is cold
fix: Usually a new thermostat with fresh coolant; replace the coolant temperature sensor if it reads wrong.
examples: Often shows up in cold weather as an aging thermostat starts sticking partly open
drive: Usually drivable. The engine is running cooler than it should, so expect weak heat and slightly worse fuel economy. In cold weather a weak defroster can block your view, so get it fixed before winter. If the gauge ever reads high or you see steam, pull over and shut it off.
test_first: Check coolant level, compare the coolant sensor reading to actual engine temperature, watch how long warm-up takes, and confirm the fan isn't stuck on before replacing the thermostat.

title: Barometric Pressure Too Low
plain: The computer is seeing an outside air pressure reading that's lower than it should be. This usually means the barometric or MAP sensor is reading wrong.
checks: Compare the barometric reading with key on, engine off to the actual local air pressure
Inspect the sensor connector, wiring and any hose
fix: Usually a new barometric or MAP sensor, or a wiring repair.
